kills.flaw: No path out of founder hours. The founder hand-buys a graded card for every order, then boxes and ships it. The ~$55 gross margin per $109 order meets a ~$38 median Meta cost per purchase, which leaves ~$17 before that labor. Volume grows only as the founder works more, and Pokemon IP limits on ad creative cap how far paid social can scale.

The founder's live camera hours are the product, so output stops when he does. The loop also never closes: people who bring a shoebox for a free appraisal are not Whatnot's buying audience, and Whatnot discovery favors established sellers. If the format doesn't take off, it falls back to a me-too singles stream that needs bought inventory, which is the flipping model every member already killed.

upgrades.upgrade: Skip guessing per-packet prices and charge the 7-10% finder's fee on close that national vintage buyers already pay (Invest In Baseball publicly pays 10%). The dealer's willingness to pay is then proven on day 1. Send each qualified packet to 2-3 vetted dealers and give the seller the competing offers, since offers on the same collection differ by 30-50%. That gives sellers a reason to submit, keeps dealers honest and protects reviews. Disclose the finder's fee on the intake form. Run triage, routing and invoicing as a daily Claude Routine on an Artifact db, so the founder's only job is vetting dealers.

Make 'refer' the default route, not the leftover. Anything outside a 60-mile radius, over the bankroll or outside the founder's expertise goes to the first-principles-3 dealer network, so revenue scales with ad spend instead of founder hands and capital. Run the funnel nationally on mail-in with prepaid insured labels, so there are no pickups. Hire a per-hour local helper on Upwork for scanning and shipping by month 3. The founder then only approves offers and takes calls on deals over $2k.

Run paid seller-intent search from day 1. Google Keyword Planner shows 25-40k searches a month at $1-5 CPC, while programmatic SEO takes 6-12 months to rank. Build fewer, richer set-value pages (real checklists and sold comps) instead of 2,000 thin ones, so Google's scaled-content-abuse policy doesn't deindex the site. Make the shareable triage report the real loop: every report carries a 'get a second opinion on your own box' link.

Fold this into first-principles-3 as the local-shop tier of one exchange, not a separate brand. Bill a finder's fee on close or per qualified lead with a junk-wax refund, have the shop pay ad spend directly, and keep the city SEO pages under one consumer brand you own. Shops then rent your traffic and never own it.
Same engine as business-mind-2 and first-principles-3, so merge them. Keep its 'first 3 qualified sellers free' risk reversal as the dealer and shop onboarding offer for the combined exchange.

Don't sell it first. Run it as the in-house listing pipeline for the desk's own inventory until it reaches 98%+ variant accuracy on real lots. Then sell it per card to estate liquidators and the exchange's partner dealers, who are warm leads already, rather than cold-pitching cash-tight shops.

Productize the work as a fixed-scope weekly bulk-sheet audit that a Claude Routine produces from exported reports, keeping the founder under 1 hr per client. Treat it as the zero-capital cash floor while the collection funnel proves its numbers, not as the main business.

Position it as the bulk sink for the collection desk, not a standalone business. Pay a local helper per assembled unit from the first order so the founder never assembles bundles, and run only during the Q4 window.
Keep it as a near-zero-founder-hour option Claude builds and runs. Add the TCGplayer affiliate and email capture from week 1, and hold to the month-4 traffic kill rule.

combo: Seller-Intent Exchange: one AI-triaged intake funnel and three exits, so every hour of founder work is spread across every lead. Intake: paid search on seller-intent terms (the founder's PPC skill), growth-1's set-value pages and shareable reports, and the estate-liquidator partner loop. A daily Claude Routine triages every submission and routes it three ways. (A) High-value lots within the home radius and the bankroll: the founder buys at about 55% or consigns at 20-25% (business-2 / leverage-1). (B) Qualified lots outside the radius or over the bankroll: an AI deal packet goes to 2-3 vetted dealers or territory shops for a 7-10% finder's fee on close (first-principles-3 / business-mind-2 / marketing-3). (C) Junk wax: a free honest report, with bulk referred to a partner shop or the demand-2 bundles. The listing pipeline (leverage-3) runs in-house on inventory the desk buys. Founder bucket: approve offers, home-radius buys and dealer vetting. Everything else is Claude, a Routine or a per-hour helper. Past $10k/mo, the business grows by adding ad budget and dealers, not founder hours or capital.
message: Most of us proposed the same profit pool, so the real question is which version stops scaling with the founder's hands and bankroll. A pure collection buyer tops out around 8-10 deals a month of founder labor. An exchange that buys only the best lots and sells every other qualified lead to dealers scales with ad budget and dealer count. I voted for the variants that monetize every lead and build owned assets (the dealer network, the pages, the triage data), not the ones that make him a busier dealer. Validate it in the first $1-1.5k of ad spend on cost per qualified lead before anyone deploys inventory capital.
